identity.title: Cross-environment Cooperation Enables Zero-shot Multi-agent Coordination

problem.claim: Enable zero-shot coordination with unfamiliar partners across unfamiliar cooperative tasks.

gap.claim: Prior approaches specialized to a single task and therefore did not generalize to new tasks, including similar ones.

contributions.claim: Introduces Cross-Environment Cooperation (CEC), training with one partner across a distribution of environments to develop general cooperative skills.
Introduces two JAX-based procedural generators for creating billions of solvable coordination challenges.
Reports that CEC outperforms competitive baselines quantitatively and qualitatively when collaborating with real people.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish CEC as a new paradigm for cross-environment cooperation and propose procedural generators at billion-challenge scale.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report quantitative and qualitative outperformance over competitive baselines in collaboration with real people.
The authors report that agents trained across many unique scenarios develop general norms that are effective with different partners.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames zero-shot adaptation to new cooperative partners as important for human-compatible AI.
Identifies single-task cooperative training as insufficient for generalization to new tasks.
Studies reinforcement learning across an environment distribution with a single partner, targeting transfer to many partners and problems.
Provides two procedural JAX generators capable of producing billions of solvable coordination challenges.
Presents CEC results against baselines and connects cross-scenario training to general norms and human interaction without human data.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly aligns training diversity—many environments—with the intended transfer target of many new partners and problems.

lessons.interpretation: Matching variation in training conditions to variation at deployment can make a generalization claim more concrete.
lessons.application: Define training and evaluation axes separately, then report whether held-out variation spans both task environments and interaction partners.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when deployment conditions are fixed or when diversity introduces solvability, optimization, or compute constraints that dominate the result.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the environments, partner-training setup, baseline identities, metrics, effect sizes, or statistical conditions behind the reported outperformance.
It does not detail how general norms are measured or how the claim about avoiding human data is experimentally established.
